question.prompt: What is the value of the expression \[ \begin{aligned} &\frac1{\log_2 100!}+\frac1{\log_3 100!}\\ &\quad+\frac1{\log_4 100!}+\cdots\\ &\qquad+\frac1{\log_{100}100!}? \end{aligned} \]

solutions.explanation:
Changing every logarithm to base \(2\) gives the terms a common denominator. Let
\[
N=100!=1\cdot2\cdot3\cdots100.
\]
For each integer \(j\) from \(2\) through \(100\), the change-of-base formula gives
\[
\frac{1}{\log_j N}
=\frac{\log_2 j}{\log_2 N}.
\]
All bases exceed \(1\), and \(N>1\), so the logarithms are defined and the denominators are nonzero. The requested sum is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\log_2 2+\cdots+\log_2 100}{\log_2 N}
&=\frac{\log_2(2\cdot3\cdots100)}{\log_2 N}\\
&=\frac{\log_2 N}{\log_2 N}=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the product rule combines the numerator, and omitting the factor \(1\) does not change \(100!\). Thus the value is \(\boxed{1}\), choice C.
solutions.title: Change to a common logarithm base
